name: sendfile
synopsis: ssize_t sendfile(int out_fd, int in_fd, off_t *_Nullable offset, size_t count);
description: sendfile() copies data between two file descriptors directly in the kernel, making it more efficient than using read(2) and write(2). It requires an input file descriptor for reading and an output for writing, with an optional offset to specify the starting point.

parameters.name: out_fd
parameters.description: Output file descriptor opened for writing

parameters.name: in_fd
parameters.description: Input file descriptor opened for reading, supporting mmap-like operations

parameters.name: offset
parameters.description: Pointer to a variable holding the file offset; if NULL, uses and updates the file offset of in_fd

parameters.name: count
parameters.description: Number of bytes to copy between the file descriptors

return_value.success: Returns the number of bytes written to out_fd; may be less than requested, requiring retries
return_value.failure: Returns -1 on error, and errno is set

errors.description: Nonblocking I/O has been selected and the write would block
The input file was not opened for reading or the output file was not opened for writing
Descriptor is not valid or locked, or an mmap-like operation is not available for in_fd, or count is negative, or out_fd has the O_APPEND flag set
Unspecified error while reading from in_fd
Insufficient memory to read from in_fd
Count is too large, exceeding the maximum size of the input or output file
Offset is not NULL but the input file is not seekable

bugs: sendfile() has varying semantics and prototypes across UNIX systems, making it unsuitable for portable programs. Additionally, there are limitations based on kernel versions, such as restrictions on file descriptor types before Linux 2.6.33.
